title: The Deadly London Acid Fog of 1952

beats.headline: THE INVISIBLE CINEMA
beats.voiceover: In December 1952, Londoners walked into movie theaters only to find the screen completely invisible—because the smog had seeped inside the building.
beats.visual_action: Establishing shot of London engulfed in deep yellow pea-soup fog; Nelson's column fades into a murky silhouette as lantern light halos.

beats.headline: 4,000 CITIZENS DEAD
beats.voiceover: Within five days, four thousand citizens were dead. But this wasn't an enemy wartime chemical attack. It was ordinary living room fireplace smoke.
beats.visual_action: Police officer guiding blind pedestrians through the choking fog near Big Ben; red warning casualty counter punches down.

beats.headline: THE THERMAL CEILING
beats.voiceover: A freak atmospheric inversion trapped a layer of freezing air over the Thames valley. A warm ceiling sat at two hundred meters, locking all smoke beneath it like a glass lid.
beats.visual_action: Battersea Power Station chimneys pumping coal smoke straight into an impenetrable thermal boundary layer.

beats.headline: DROPLETS OF ACID
beats.voiceover: Every day, London burned thousands of tons of high-sulfur coal. Inside the dense fog droplets, sulfur dioxide reacted with nitrogen, catalyzing into airborne sulfuric acid.
beats.visual_action: Macro push-in to microscopic water droplets; chemical reaction callout SO2 + H2O -> H2SO4 acid mist.

beats.headline: MORTALITY QUADRUPLED
beats.voiceover: When the government plotted air samples against morgue intake, the curves matched in absolute lockstep. As sulfur levels peaked, daily deaths quadrupled.
beats.visual_action: The authentic 1953 Wilkins mortality chart slams into view; yellow highlighter and red ink callout target the lethal week 49 spike.

beats.headline: CLEAN AIR ACT 1956
beats.voiceover: The deadly yellow fog forced Parliament to ban smoky fuels in cities forever, giving birth to the modern environmental movement.
beats.visual_action: The fog lifts as parliament passes the Clean Air Act 1956; clean blue sky and historical archival stamp lock onto the frame.
